links.outcome: Output reproducibility across repeated runs and stability across prompt formats (naive vs structured)
links.effect: Internal reproducibility (ICC >0.500) and distributional stability across prompts were high, but this consistency was based on nondiscriminatory safety biases, masking failure to identify high-risk patients.
links.quote: While internal reproducibility (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICCs] >0.500) and distributional stability across prompts were surprisingly high, this consistency proved deceptive, based entirely on nondiscriminatory safety biases.

links.outcome: Calibration (Brier score) versus discrimination (sensitivity) of LLM outcome predictions
links.effect: DS naive Brier score 0.068 at 6 months suggested high probabilistic accuracy, but all models had sensitivity 0.00 at 6-month and 1-year horizons; calibration masked discriminatory failure.
links.quote: However, this mathematical precision masked a failure in clinical utility: all models exhibited a sensitivity of 0.00 at 6-month and 1-year horizons.

screen.reason: The study retrospectively evaluates LLM prognostic performance and explicitly compares structured (tabular) versus naive zero-shot prompting strategies, highlighting risks around calibration and discrimination for clinical prognostication.
